source.title: Quantifying task-relevant representational similarity using decision variable correlation
source.authors: Qian Yu; Wilson S. Geisler; Xuexin Wei

record.tranche_reason: The study measures task-relevant representational similarity across monkey brain areas and vision models, and reports lower model–brain similarity for more accurate, adversarially trained, and data-rich models. It also finds model similarity varies by model family and compares similarity metrics.
record.gate_note: The paper's own DVC, Cohen's Kappa, and RSA analyses are recorded below. Results cited from other studies are not included. The paper's method description and implementation choices are not results; the raw-pixel comparison and other findings that do not measure the claim versions are omitted.
record.test_reason: The model–model DVC results bear on V7 and V6. ImageNet-1k models trained on the same data do not converge beyond monkey–monkey levels, and similarity clusters by architecture family and training procedure. The decoder comparison shows that model–model Cohen's Kappa depends on decoder choice. The model–brain results, which are the paper's headline, measure a different construct from the model–model versions and are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right, with additions. The authors find model–model DVC comparable to monkey–monkey DVC, while model–monkey DVC is lower and declines with ImageNet accuracy. Adversarial training markedly increases model–model similarity but not model–brain similarity, and larger pretraining data does not help. Architecture and training still shape model solutions. Kappa-based reports of high model–model consistency partly reflect decoder bias.
record.recipe_differences: The study introduces DVC, decoding task-relevant decision variables with LDA and correlating them, rather than reproducing the original sources' representational-similarity or convergence measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: The study compares DVC with Cohen's Kappa and RSA; Cohen's Kappa changes with decoder choice and decision bias. The negative performance–DVC trend persists with Spearman correlation and other tested DVC implementation choices.

fits_no_version.finding: Model–brain (V4/IT) DVC is modest (0.29) and declines with ImageNet-1k accuracy (r=-0.70). The decline is robust to Spearman correlation, PC count, LDA solver, category-level RSA and a second monkey dataset. Adversarial (0.27) and data-rich (0.24) models are not more brain-aligned.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: More capable vision models become less aligned with primate V4/IT on task-relevant decision variables (model–brain divergence with capability).

fits_no_version.finding: In simulation, RSA plateaus as shared task-irrelevant fluctuations grow, while DVC is unaffected.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Geometry-based similarity measures can be dominated by shared task-irrelevant variance, inflating apparent alignment.

record.peer_reviewed: 39th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2025)
record.problems: The main neural comparison uses two monkeys and a limited number of simultaneously recorded neurons; the authors note that larger neural datasets would improve DVC estimates. Most model-pair cohort comparisons are not given as numerical means in the text. Generalization from macaques and the selected image stimuli is limited, and the authors caution that the objects may not have the same behavioral relevance for monkeys as for humans.
record.rows_left_out: No results-bearing rows omitted for the 60-row cap.

untested.parts: No analysis of model–model DVC as a function of scale or ImageNet accuracy. Data-rich versus representative cohorts differ in data, not in a controlled scale sweep.
No image–caption paired cross-modal comparison. CLIP is used only as an image encoder.
No mapping, stitching or relative-representation tests.
No feature- or circuit-level universality analysis.
No variation of neighbourhood size and no out-of-distribution input test of model–model DVC.
No test of a plateau with scale. No causal test of a common model of reality versus shared data.

missing.what: Model and monkey representations both have substantial DVC to raw image pixels (monkeys 0.153/0.195). The authors suggest part of the DVC reflects linear separability already present in the inputs, a shared-input cause relevant to V7.
Model–model DVC among representative models on the Bashivan et al. dataset (shown only as a heatmap, no numbers).

record.verdict_notes: The paper's headline results are model–brain, which none of the versions name, so most rows are delinked. Only the model–model DVC and the metric-comparison rows bear on V6/V7. Neither original source is this study. The paper cites the Platonic hypothesis only as background.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether similarity between independently trained models rises with model scale or capability.
CLIP is included among data-rich models, but the study does not compare image and caption representations for paired data or test cross-modal alignment as both models improve.
No controlled comparison of networks trained from different initializations of the same architecture, or of shared features or subspaces, is reported.
The study does not test mappings, stitching, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
The study does not test recurrence of interpretable features or circuits.
The study compares DVC with Cohen's Kappa and RSA and tests some DVC implementation choices, but does not systematically vary neighbourhood settings or out-of-distribution inputs.

The study reports incomplete similarity and differences by model family and training cohort. It does not test whether model-to-model alignment plateaus with scale or establish that shared data or objectives, rather than a common model of reality, cause the observed similarity.
